endorsements.quote: The manuscript or deployment dossier should define the rare subtype, clinical setting, input data, output, target user, supported decision and limitations.

Patient-level separation must be maintained across training, validation and test sets, and all preprocessing, feature selection, augmentation, imputation, normalization and hyperparameter tuning should be performed inside the training loop.

Therefore, AUC should be accompanied by confidence intervals, precision-recall metrics, rare-subtype sensitivity, calibration slope or intercept, Brier score, decision-curve analysis where appropriate and explicit reporting of event counts.

The sixth step is a supervised clinical pilot, ideally as silent deployment, second-read support or tumor board support before clinical influence; pilot outcomes should include decision confidence, diagnostic timing, additional investigations, workflow burden and clinician override patterns.
Governance should define when clinicians are expected to override AI, including discordance with multimodal evidence, low-confidence outputs or use outside the validated population.
Monitoring should include data drift, performance drift, subgroup safety, workflow impact, user behavior, false negatives, false positives and model update governance.
Large language models may assist summarization, evidence retrieval or tumor board preparation, but they should not generate unverified treatment recommendations or replace specialist judgment.
Patient and public involvement should also be incorporated into governance.

Rather, AI should function as clinically governed decision support: a system that improves recognition, prioritization, information integration and multidisciplinary interpretation while leaving final responsibility with clinicians and tumor boards.
Overrides and disagreements should be logged for safety learning, recalibration and audit.

Authors should report the rare subtype definition, inclusion and exclusion criteria, dataset sources, sample size, event counts, class balance, reference standard, data modality, data quality, preprocessing, model development, leakage prevention, internal and external validation, performance metrics, uncertainty, calibration, subgroup analysis, error analysis, synthetic data disclosure, privacy and bias assessment, explainability, human oversight, workflow integration, lifecycle monitoring and limitations.

AI outputs should be reviewed by the relevant specialist: breast radiologists for imaging outputs, pathologists for histological outputs, molecular pathologists or genomic scientists for molecular interpretation and oncologists or tumor boards for treatment relevance.
Practice point: deployment dossiers should state the maximum safe scope of use and list contraindications, including untested subtypes, unscreened populations or unsupported workflows.
State whether the intended use may fall under medical-device or in-vitro diagnostic regulatory pathways and how monitoring will be documented.
The seventh step is governed deployment and routine use with standard operating procedures, user training, override mechanisms and documentation.

unlisted_practices: Do not use synthetic data as a substitute for real external validation, and exclude synthetic cases from test sets used to claim clinical performance.
Review synthetic data with structured, discipline-specific clinical plausibility scoring combined with quantitative fidelity, diversity, privacy and utility checks.
Report subtype-specific confusion matrices, calibration and error analysis for pan-rare pooled models rather than relying on pooled metrics.
Report the best feasible alternative validation design (temporal, leave-one-institution-out, silent prospective, registry-based) when independent external validation is unavailable.
Label validation claims as exploratory, pilot, externally validated or clinically monitored according to the evidence available.
Do not deploy AI as an autonomous diagnostic or treatment-selection system without prospective clinical oversight.
Use objective quantitative data-quality and distributional similarity checks alongside multidisciplinary review to assess data readiness.
Use site-aware splitting and leave-one-institution-out testing when pooling multi-hospital data to avoid learning institutional signatures.
Treat saliency maps and feature-importance outputs as hypothesis-generating unless stability and clinical plausibility are assessed; prefer interpretable models in small cohorts.
Curate rare breast cancer datasets through multidisciplinary review of diagnostic accuracy and subtype definition using expert-confirmed labels.
Include federated learning safeguards such as harmonized labels, quality control, privacy safeguards and site-level performance reporting.

screen.reason: This is a Perspective article proposing a clinical governance framework and recommendations for safe AI development and deployment in rare breast cancers.
